name: e02_cross_asset
title: 2. One rule, twelve markets: EMA50/200 across asset classes
text:
**Question.** Is the EMA50/200 result a property of NVDA in 2022-2025, or does the same untuned rule add value across asset classes?

**Setup.** The identical rule runs on all 12 assets over each one's full history (warm-up on prior data, next-close fills, 5 bp per side, 15 bp for Bitcoin, T-bill cash), against buy-and-hold over the same window and an *exposure-matched mix* holding the rule's average exposure in the asset and the rest in T-bills (its Sharpe equals buy-and-hold's by construction, max gap 0.000, so it is the yardstick for CAGR and drawdown).

**Findings.**

- Sharpe is higher than buy-and-hold in **6 of 12** markets (median difference -0.001); CAGR is higher in only **3 of 12** (median -1.9% a year). A paired stationary bootstrap's 95% interval for the Sharpe gap covers zero in **every** market (median half-width 0.29). Excluding the two hindsight picks (NVDA, Bitcoin), the rule wins on Sharpe in 4 of 10 ETFs and on CAGR in 3 of 10; the picks win 2 of 2 on Sharpe.
- Maximum drawdown is shallower in **12 of 12** markets, by a median 18 percentage points. Against the exposure-matched mix (median exposure 71%) the rule has a shallower drawdown in **9 of 12** (7 by more than 1 pp; median +4.5 pp) and a higher CAGR in 6 of 12.
- By class, the mean Sharpe gain is positive for US equity (+0.06), Bonds (+0.02), Crypto (+0.03, one asset) and Single stock (+0.02, one asset); zero or negative for Intl equity (-0.04), Commodities (-0.00) and Real estate (-0.16, one asset).
- The rule is slow: a median 0.7 round trips a year and a 48% hit rate, so roughly half the round trips are whipsaw losses and the long trends pay for them.
- On SPY it gave +42 and +44 percentage points of protection in the 2000-02 and 2007-09 bears, but in the COVID crash it lost 32% vs 34% for buy-and-hold, exited only at the trough (23 Mar 2020) and then missed a 44% rebound before re-entering on 10 Jun 2020. Before the August 2020 bond peak the rule **trailed** buy-and-hold TLT (Sharpe 0.32 vs 0.53); afterwards its drawdown was -17% vs -48%.

**Interpretation.** A long/flat trend rule behaves like a dynamically replicated protective put: it sells after a sustained fall and buys back after a recovery, so it truncates slow bear markets and pays a premium in whipsaws and in missed V-shaped rebounds (Fung & Hsieh 2001 model trend followers as lookback straddles). That premium shows up as the CAGR give-up; the protection shows up as drawdowns. Slow, grinding declines (US equities in 2000-02 and 2007-09, Treasuries in 2022) give the 200-day average time to react; fast crashes (COVID) and assets in a secular uptrend (Treasuries before 2020) make time out of the market close to pure opportunity cost. Monthly, up and down months are cut by similar amounts: at a monthly horizon the rule looks like a smaller position, and the option-like payoff only appears over multi-month bear markets (median upside capture 65%, downside 62%). Against the exposure-matched mix, a median 73% of the drawdown reduction is reproduced by simply holding less of the asset; the remaining timing edge (median +4.5 pp, more than 1 pp in 7 of 12 markets) is small, and section 9 tests whether it is significant in any market. Overall the evidence is no reliable risk-adjusted improvement: the Sharpe comparison is close to a coin flip. The drawdown reduction matches Faber (2007); the return give-up is less flattering than his long-history results with a monthly 10-month average. Time-series momentum is broad but modest per asset and earns its keep mainly through diversification across many markets and through shorting downtrends, which this long/flat single-asset rule does not do (Moskowitz, Ooi & Pedersen 2012; Hurst, Ooi & Pedersen 2017).
after: Histories run 11-32 years, so a single Sharpe ratio has a standard error of roughly 1/sqrt(years) = 0.18-0.30; the paired bootstrap puts the standard error of the *gap* near 0.15 (narrower, because the rule and buy-and-hold share most of their days), still far larger than the median gap. The 12 markets are also correlated (SPY, QQQ, IWM, VNQ and NVDA all load on US stocks), so the counts are not independent tests. Selection caveats: the ETFs are the long-lived survivors of their categories, and NVDA and Bitcoin are included only because they are famous winners. The matched mix rebalances daily without costs, a slight advantage to the benchmark.
